title: 'The spine just wants to move': How to strengthen your neck
content:
The modern world is a challenging place for necks. These five exercises will help you cope.
Sometimes it pays to consider the weight of the human head.
When you're sat or stood upright, the mechanical load that your head places on the neck is only about 12 pounds (5.4kg), says Anthony Ghosh, a NHS consultant spinal neurosurgeon at Queen's Hospital in London. This is not a problem.
But across the planet, billions of us are spending large portions of our day with our bodies hunched over. And as we stoop over our laptops and smartphones, we're radically changing the distribution of weight on our necks.
In this uncomfortable, downward-looking position, the load the head places on the neck goes up to about 60 pounds (27.2kg), says Ghosh. "So, it's quite a lot of strain that your neck is trying to put up with."
In short, modern life is terrible for our necks. But there are five simple exercises you can try to keep your neck healthy and prevent problems down the line, whatever your age.
Some neck problems are a natural consequence of changes which play out across our musculoskeletal system as we age, resulting in diminishing elasticity and increasing stiffness within the neck's supportive tissues.
"Nobody above the age of 40 has a normal MRI scan when it comes to their spine," says Ghosh. "Everybody will have some worn discs, the cushions between vertebrae. The joints at the back of the neck also thicken up a little bit and get stiff."
Then there's the impact of technology. When we pore over electronic devices, we adopt a characteristic "flexed" posture . The upper back rounds into an exaggerated hunch or hump, and the chin and head push forward instead of aligning directly over the shoulders. This puts a large amount of strain on both the neck muscles and the vertebrae joints in the upper spine.
Anywhere between 60% and 80% of people will suffer from neck pain during their lifetime, with nearly 50% experiencing it as a frequent or recurring issue. These problems might begin with an increasing sense of stiffness and lack of mobility in your upper spine, followed by growing and persistent levels of discomfort.
Alarmingly, research suggests that neck and upper back-related problems are beginning to arise earlier in life. The prevalence of scoliosis has steadily increased in children and adolescents over the past three decades, for example. This medical condition involves developing an abnormal curvature of the spine, forcing the neck muscles to strain and compensate to keep the head level.
But there is plenty that we can do to mitigate the onset of neck problems. Rather than investing in upper chairs or other ergonomic aids, Ghosh simply recommends moving more and ensuring that you take more breaks from looking at screens. "The spine just wants to move," he says. "It means that the circulation flows through it, and the muscles get more tone in them."
In particular, the below exercises can help loosen the joints, correct bad posture and make your neck muscles more resilient to the challenges of staring forwards at a screen. Always consult your doctor before attempting a new exercise regime.
If you are suffering from neck pain, the NHS recommends a simple exercise to help get strength and movement back. While sitting upright or lying on your back, look as far to the right as far as you can and hold for two seconds. You should feel a stretch on the opposite side of your neck. Return to the starting position and then look to the left as far as you can. Repeat this two or three times, and as often throughout the day as feels comfortable.
Maintaining good neck posture is very important, as poor posture places strain on your neck muscles. Our necks are designed to move in all directions, so one tip is to move it around regularly throughout the day.
However, the 'optimal' position for your neck is in a neutral position in line with your spine. Keep your shoulders and back relaxed and your neck long and upright. Try to avoid poking your chin forwards and rounding your shoulders, and avoid keeping your head twisted or tilted to the side for long periods.
It helps to adopt this posture when sitting for long periods, such as when working at a computer, watching television, or driving.
Spending years gazing at a computer screen can lead to a 'poking chin' posture, where your head juts forward instead of being aligned over your shoulders. However, this can be corrected by changing your sitting habits and doing simple exercises.
One thing you can do is gently lengthen your neck upwards as you tuck in your chin. It helps to imagine a soft peach under your chin. You don't want to squash it by tucking in too hard, but equally don't let it drop. Widen your collar bones and gently draw your shoulder blades down and back centrally towards your spine. At the same time, gently pull in your lower 'core' tummy muscles to maintain a natural soft curve in your lower back.

title: I only found out I had cancer after my four-year-old kicked me in the testicles
content:
Ben Lidgey was "messing around" with his son in the garden when he was accidentally kicked in the testicles - but it may well have saved his life.
When he was still in pain after a week, he sought medical help and found out he had testicular cancer.
A new report from men's charity Movember says a third of men in Wales die before their 75th birthday, and calls on the Welsh government to develop a dedicated plan for men's health.
The government said its existing suicide prevention and self harm, mental health and cancer strategies are already working to tackle some of the challenges facing men.
Warning: This article discusses suicide
Lidgey, from Cardiff, says his testicle felt "like a cricket ball" after being kicked by his son, but he was reluctant to see his GP, thinking the problem would go away.
"It's one of those fairly typical things that happens to men and you shrug it off and think, 'well, it'll get better'," he said.
"I was in a busy family environment, you know, two small children, there were lots of other things going on."
After being given the all-clear for cancer, Lidgey faced a different challenge.
He said: "I felt like I was fine but after five years my wife said 'I don't think you are fine. I think you need to talk to somebody'.
"She was picking up on the fact that I was perhaps a bit shorter, a bit more argumentative, less patient with people and just not the same person I was before."
After counselling, Lidgey saw an improvement, and is now an advocate for more support for men and boys.
A reluctance to seek help for both physical and mental health is often cited as a reason why men, in general, die younger.
Movember's report says almost 7,000 men died before their 75th birthday in 2024. The rate of premature death in women is significantly lower at 28%.
Often, it says, men die from preventable conditions or those likely to benefit from earlier treatment such as certain cancers, heart, lung and liver diseases, those related to drugs and alcohol as well as suicide.
Where a man lives also matters, with the premature mortality rate in Blaenau Gwent about 60% higher than in Powys, while men in the most deprived communities can expect to live 7.5 years less than those in the least deprived.
The analysis also suggest the costs to the Welsh economy of the top five causes of male premature death is £1.4bn a year.
Jonathan Scourfield, professor of Social Care at Cardiff University, said: "Young men, in particular, are much more likely to get injured and die from physical risk taking. The expectation of physical strength."
He said some men may also ignore the importance of building up a social network or rely on a female partner to take care of that.
"And then, if they're widowed or if they retire, they really struggle with loneliness," he said.

Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether. That’s according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology , which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments. “We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer,” said Gary Clifford, the study’s senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. “We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works,” Clifford said. “It’s an awareness-raising issue.” About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024. Other infections contributed substantially as well: “Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development,” Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email. “However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV,” Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available. Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory’s Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set. The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018 , but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV. “EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma,” Clifford said. “That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we’ve identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas,” he said. “We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn’t really fully addressed because we didn’t understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing.” The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn’t evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment. But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives. “Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later,” said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study. “Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States,” she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV. “Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer,” Fedirko said. “Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures.” Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference. Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops. Getting tested and following up with a doctor “almost takes away any cancer risk,” Clifford said. Once infections get diagnosed, “we know how to manage them,” he said. “The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we’re learning more about which ones, but that’s a work in progress. The point is: It doesn’t mean that you’ve got a cancer just because you have the infection.” For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road. The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop. Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection. HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses , which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer : cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection. The new research “teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer,” Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email. “This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced,” Lee said. “Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower.” Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include “safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis,” Rumgay said. “If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide.”

Like the rest of my Gen X peers, I grew up with the message that striving for the “Buns of Steel” body was about how you looked in a leotard, not how much weight you could squat in the gym. Women were actively discouraged from strength training for fear of becoming bulky. For women, cardio has been king — or should we say queen? — for decades, but new awareness of the health benefits of building muscle , particularly for those in middle age, has led more women to start lifting weights. Strength training can be important to protect bone density and overall well-being as we get older. New pressure to lift heavy and count protein grams to build muscle mass can lead to another problem for some women, however: an unhealthy preoccupation with exercise and food and yet another aspirational appearance standard. Women need to know how to care for their bodies without falling prey to unrealistic expectations that can undermine their well-being. Liz Bucar , a professor of religion at Northeastern University in Boston, used to experience fitness through a cardio-only lens, “always trying to be smaller.” In midlife now, “we’re all being told, actually, oops, all that advice was terrible,” said Bucar, author of “ Beyond Wellness : How Restoring the Religious Roots of Spiritual Practices Can Heal Us.” “Your bones are disintegrating because you didn’t have your period because you were just on the stair machine for hours a day.” Bucar, who now strength trains with a coach, described this shift from counting calories to progressing in the weight room as powerful because it is “more protective of our health” and “pushes back against conventional beauty norms.” “I love the idea that we’re creating this whole generation of grandmas who can’t knit and bake or whatever but are the first in our line of ancestors who can lift our husbands over our heads,” Bucar said. Strength training can be a way for women to heal their relationship with physical activity and their body, according to fitness journalist Mikala Jamison , who writes the Body Type newsletter and is the author of the forthcoming book “ The Forever Project : How Exercise Strengthened Me Inside and Out for the Long Haul.” “For so many of us, exercise was this very toxic thing when it came to our bodies and our mindset, and how it was entwined with diet culture ,” Jamison told me. “Taking care of yourself through fitness feels like inarguably a good thing to do. It’s women taking up space.” Even though Jamison credits strength training as a critical part of her own eating disorder recovery, she still has concerns about the framing of this fitness trend. “‘Strong is the new skinny’ should be like a Bat-Signal to somebody like me, right? Like, oh, that sounds so great. But I think it’s also very complicated,” she said. Even though women of all sizes are trying to build strength, the images on social media suggest “it’s all about strong and skinny. It’s just another body standard that can be very damaging,” Jamison said. “More women are strength training than ever before in America. The benefits of that can’t be overstated,” she said. “But at the same time, the face of that message is often women who are still objectively small, just with some additional obvious musculature.” Keri Harvey, a certified personal trainer and co-owner of Form Fitness Brooklyn in New York, agreed that larger women who lift weights are underrepresented in our culture. “You’re seeing people in smaller bodies who have muscles, and they are strong, and that’s amazing,” Harvey said. “And yet there are people in larger bodies who are strong as well, and their bodies also have cellulite. Their bodies also have fat. And it may not look like the person that you’re seeing on Instagram or the magazine cover, but that is still a strong body.” Building strength is often literally at odds with shrinking the body. “I like to tell people to remember that muscles need room,” Harvey said. “Our lats, as they get stronger, it may mean we have to go up in a bra size. Or as your biceps get stronger, it might mean your shirt that you were expecting to fit more loosely might be a bit more snug.” Harvey encouraged women “to be comfortable with the idea that your body is going to change as you get stronger, but it may not change in the way that you think it should and that’s not a bad thing. It’s tough because a lot of us have been taught that we have to be small.” While the popularity of strength training is getting more women into the weight room, it can also feed into a “very aspirational body standard,” Jamison said. “Sometimes it feels like we’re just constantly shuffling these cards of what is the look to have, but we’re just calling it different things all the time. Like, OK, it’s about strength, but, really, is it? Or is it about just being really, really lean?” The physical and mental health risks of getting swept up by a fitness trend are a concern to Megan Hellner , a registered dietitian and cofounder of AthleatMD , a medical and nutrition treatment program for athletes with relative energy deficiency in sport, or RED-S , and eating disorders. “It feels like we’re trading one very narrow body ideal for another,” she said. While Hellner warned about the risks of trying to change your body to match what she refers to as the “athletic aesthetic,” she acknowledged the upside of an emphasis on strength over thinness is that “it does at least require an input of energy. Muscle is very expensive tissue to build and maintain calorically.” In contrast to an emphasis on thinness that led many women to restrict calories, a focus on lifting weights simply isn’t compatible with dieting. “Strength and building muscle require that we eat. We have to feed the muscles, and so a lot of the categories of foods that have been demonized in other trends are things that we need in order to build the muscle,” Harvey said. Rather than carefully monitoring their body on a scale, some women find themselves fixating on a different kind of weight, as they strive for increasing the amount they can lift in a training approach called “progressive overload. ” For those who find their relationship to strength training is becoming obsessive, Harvey invited them to remember that “our main goal should be for us to feel strong enough to live our lives,” Harvey said. “If we’re so focused on never feeling like we are doing enough, then it takes the joy away from lifting.” Hellner advised women to watch out for “ignoring whispers from the body before they become screams. If there’s pain or injury and someone is not honoring their body and resting, that is a red flag, or if there is quite a bit of distress when they’re not able to strength train on a given day.” For someone used to going hard on the cardio machines every day, Harvey noted that the schedule for strength training can take some getting used to. “Your body needs rest just as much as it needs the strength training. We don’t want to fatigue the muscles constantly,” she said. “We want to give them time to learn a pattern, to be comfortable with a load, and then we can move on.” Without adequate rest, lifting weights can “just tear the body down.” When it comes to nutrition for strength training, Hellner encouraged women to avoid seeing food only as something that supports their fitness routine and instead “thinking about fueling for all of the reasons we need food: basic life processing, hormone production, organ function, all activities of daily living, including connecting with people, building community, experiencing joy.” Both Harvey and Jamison emphasized the importance of finding the right balance and a routine based on your personal needs. A woman who wants to feel less creaky in daily life doesn’t have to approach strength training like she’s preparing for a powerlifting competition. While this fitness trend might be getting more women to start lifting, Harvey said she wanted them to find sustainable ways to pursue their goals that go beyond appearance or a fitness fad. “It is so encouraging to be able to walk into a gym, and in the free weights section, I’m not the only woman there,” she said. “That is a really cool and exciting thing, and I just am hopeful that it continues, and that it’s not something that drops off when the trend changes because it will. It always does.” Separating exercise from appearance can be the best way to find a health-promoting, personal connection to movement. It’s why Jamison argued for a much more inclusive approach than is typically portrayed online. “I don’t think the only way fitness should be appreciated or commendable is if it results in a lean and very obviously muscular body,” she said. “That should not be the only picture of health, strength or fitness.” Note: If you or someone you know may be struggling with an eating disorder, the National Alliance for Eating Disorders provides free resources and referrals.

In a cosmic first, scientists say they have detected a planet that may have formed from the burned remains of its dead host star. The planet is likely a gas giant orbiting a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832 located about 270 light-years from Earth , according to the authors of a study published Monday in the journal Nature Astronomy. After analyzing observations from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and other instruments, the team found chemical evidence that suggests the planet could have condensed from material expelled by the star as it fizzled out of energy and collapsed into a white dwarf. When a sunlike star dies, it first rapidly expands into a red giant and then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a much smaller but dense, hot core — known as a white dwarf. Some of the first-generation planets, those that originally formed at the same time as the star, can survive this cataclysmic event if their orbit is wide enough. Astronomers have observed a handful of such first-generation survivors revolving around white dwarfs, but never before have they recorded a so-called second-generation planet — an entirely new world made from a dead star’s debris. The telltale sign that HS 0209+0832 might have birthed a new planet is unusual traces of heavy elements on the white dwarf’s surface that the study authors believe is planetary material raining down onto the leftover core. “This planetary material is very rich in an element called niobium,” said lead study author Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in the department of physics of the University of Warwick in England. “It’s the first time that this element is found in a white dwarf, and this implies that the planetary material is made from the ashes of the star as it died.” Further analysis of observations from NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite or TESS revealed a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days — evidence that the researchers say is consistent with a giant planet orbiting the white dwarf. “What’s interesting about planets orbiting close to white dwarfs is that because white dwarfs cool over time, their habitable zone is very stable. A second-generation planet could form and then be in the habitable zone for tens of billions of years,” Williams said. Such a large period of stability could provide more ideal conditions for life, but more work is required to validate the second-generation planet discovery, he added. “It’s not a confirmed planet,” Williams said. “It’s only a candidate for now.” After the red giant phase when a dying star quickly puffs up, it becomes a nuclear furnace that can produce various elements. However, once that fuel runs out and the star transforms into a white dwarf, the heavy elements — including nobium — sink downward rapidly, leaving only lighter elements such as hydrogen and helium on the surface. The researchers determined that the niobium detected on HS 0209+0832 must therefore come from the star’s surroundings. “We think these elements fell onto the white dwarf’s surface because the white dwarf is very hot and emitting loads of extreme ultraviolet radiation, which is stripping the atmosphere of a nearby planet,” Williams said. The idea of second-generation planets has existed for at least as long as astronomers have known about exoplanets, said study coauthor David J. Wilson, a research associate at the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder. Scientists detected the very first exoplanets around a pulsar — a type of rapidly rotating dead star — and because pulsars form as a result of massive explosions called supernovas, these planets are likely second-generation, as any original planets would have been destroyed by the immense blast, Wilson explained. “Although white dwarfs don’t form via supernova, they are surrounded by debris,” he said via email. “You have the planets that were lucky enough to survive the star’s giant phases, the shattered remains of those that weren’t, and leftover gas and dust ejected by the star as it turned from a giant to a white dwarf. So it’s a compelling idea that all that stuff might coalesce into new planets.” Astronomers still don’t know all the details about how first-generation planets form, which means the potential mechanisms behind this newly reported second-generation planet are even more uncertain. The planet-forming process might have derived from a collision between the dying star and a second celestial body, according to Williams. “There could have been another object close to the core of the star, maybe a star around 20% the mass of the sun, or a brown dwarf,” said Williams, referring to a class of cool objects that are an intermediate between a star and a planet. If a second object fell into the star during its giant phase, it could have prevented all the dust and gas from spreading out into a massive cloud, making some of it spin in a disk. This disk would then have continued to rotate around the white dwarf, birthing a planet. “In a regular white dwarf there’s no disc, because the star’s material will just be ejected outwards during the red giant phase,” Williams added. The researchers plan to use Hubble and NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to observe the system again over the next year, but they also requested time with the more powerful James Webb Space Telescope, which could provide more clues about the existence or features of the planet. If confirmed, this distant world would belong to an entirely new planetary class and suggest that more second-generation planets could exist around white dwarfs, Williams said. The discovery would also have implications for our own cosmic neighborhood, Wilson said. “The sun will eventually become a white dwarf, so we’re also looking at the future of the solar system here — maybe the Sun will get a new planet someday!” The new discovery of a potential second-generation planet is incredibly exciting, said Sarah Casewell, a lecturer at the School of Physics and Astronomy of the University of Leicester, England, who was not involved with the study. “We know of a large number of white dwarfs that are polluted by planetary material which is similar in composition to rocks within our solar system,” she wrote in an email. “However, in this case, the white dwarf is polluted by incredibly unusual material and the composition of this material is similar to atoms we see being created as stars end their lives.” More than 95% of all stars in the universe will eventually become white dwarfs, and astronomers have already cataloged hundreds of thousands of them. Finding a planet that has formed after the white dwarf would mean that second-generation planets around other white dwarfs are possible — and that after our sun dies, new planets could emerge in our own solar system, Casewell said. Previous observations of white dwarfs have shown that some planetary systems survive a star’s self-destruction, but the recent findings open the possibility of the genesis of new planets, said Amy Bonsor, an associate professor at the University of Cambridge in England, who also did not participate in the work. “This paradigm shift allows us to consider whether in the future we could characterise or investigate the potential habitability of these second-generation planetary systems,” she wrote in an email. This discovery would also add more evidence to research that has shown planetary systems are varied and complex, even after the host star dies, according to Susan Mullally, a mission scientist at the Space Telescope Science Institute, the science operations center for Hubble. “Some planets may survive the death of the star, others may be tossed into space or eaten by the star. If second-generation planets are possible, then many more white dwarf stars will have planets than we may otherwise expect,” Mullally, who was not part of the study, wrote in an email. “This evidence of a second-generation exoplanet indicates there may be more to the afterlives of exoplanets than previously expected.”

The 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine has been awarded to three scientists – Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel – for their work developing a technique to decode the inner workings of the brain. This method – known as optogenetics – acts as a “light-sensitive switch,” allowing scientists to “map which cells are responsible for which function” in the brain, said Anna Wedell, a member of the Nobel Prize committee, which announced the prestigious honor in Sweden on Monday. German researchers Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, discovered a protein in algae, known as channelrhodopsin, before American scientist Deisseroth, 54, “transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells,” the committee said in a statement. That work has “laid the foundation for a new era in neuroscience,” the committee added. By using this method, researchers can identify and even control the neural circuits that govern “specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.” Two of the laureates have shared their surprise to winning this year’s prize. Deisseroth had been working on a paper and only just gone to bed when the Nobel committee called him to give him the good news, he said in a telephone interview shared on the Nobel Prize website. “Now I don’t think I’ll be able to sleep for quite a while,” he added. Nagel, meanwhile, spoke of his surprise at learning he was a recipient this year while “on the terrace, in the sun” in Italy. “I didn’t expect this, really!” he said. “I have some friends who always say they are watching what’s happening in October when they are announcing it, and I always told them ‘Keep cool.’ There’s only, so far, I know of one patient who profited from optogenetics so … I thought it’s still too early to get this prize in medicine.” The award highlights the “profound impact of a field that has fundamentally changed how scientists understand the brain and nervous system,” said David Pendlebury, head of research analysis at Clarivate’s Institute for Scientific Information, in a statement. “The Nobel Committee’s recognition underscores the extraordinary influence of this work, which has transformed neuroscience by enabling researchers to use light to precisely control and study neural activity,” Pendlebury added. The discovery began with Hegemann’s curiosity about the behavior of single-celled algae known as Chlamydomonas , which are able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein found on the surface of Chlamydomonas that is unusually both light-sensitive and generates electrical impulses. Regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive. Deisseroth, who still works as a psychiatrist alongside his research, built on their discovery by introducing the gene that codes the protein into the nerve cells of rats. By illuminating the nerve cells, he was able around 2007 to control the movement of mouse whiskers. The work marked the infancy of the field of optogenetics, which now means that researchers can understand which nerve cells in the brain control different functions. For example, the Nobel committee said scientists have since identified neural circuits that govern pain, social behaviors, thirst, food consumption, reward and attention. Finding a way to learn about the role of specific brain regions in mental functions “transformed how we study malfunctioning circuits in mental disorders,” said Andrea Benucci, a professor in biology and experimental psychology at Queen Mary University of London, in an email. “The ability to activate or silence neurons in the brain using laser light has opened the door to unprecedented precision,” Benucci told CNN. The hope is optogenetics will lead to new medical treatments as well as a deeper understanding of psychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Researchers in optogenetics are attempting to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye’s rods and cones. “When they inserted a channelrhodopsin-like protein in the retina of a blind person, the person regained some vision. Using special glasses emitting light, the person was able to discern and grasp objects on a table,” according to a release from the Nobel committee. Another area of research seeks to harness optogenetics to improve cochlear implants for hearing loss. The three laureates will equally split the 12 million Swedish krona ($1,200,000) prize pot. Four more Nobel Prizes – physics, chemistry, literature and peace – will be awarded later this week, before the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Science is awarded next Monday. This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.
